title: Where the Tokens Go: Heat, Entropy and Error in Agentic Coding
comments: 43 pages, 10 figures, 11 tables; includes supplementary information with 3 further figures
summary: Coding agents are billed by the token, yet software engineering says nothing about what a token actually buys. Here we introduce a theory of software thermodynamics. The theory draws analogues from classical and stochastic thermodynamics, extends them, and applies them to modern agentic coding. We count the tokens an agent generates as its cost and divide that cost into work and heat. The test suite acts as a software Maxwell's daemon that judges every coding change. We test the theory with an analogue of the experiments in which a single molecule is pulled open and let fold again: an agent makes a change to a repository (coding) and then undoes it (uncoding), many times over, and we count the tokens of every model call. The cycle returns the requested edits to where they began, with each direction started from a stored reference tree, and the spread of its cost over repeated cycles defines a software temperature, which rose with the sampling temperature of the model. About 80 per cent of the tokens of a successful run are generated in model calls that leave the requested change where it was, and we call these tokens heat. The free energy of a change, which we estimate by analogy with the equality of Jarzynski, is 14 to 22 per cent of the mean cost of a successful coding run. Coding costs 1.1 to 1.5 times as much as uncoding. The daemon is imperfect: the verdict of a test suite varies with its environment, and a suite that accepts a broken change has a cost in tokens. The practical implication of the proposed theory could be new tools for analysing and optimising coding agents through the lens of thermodynamics.

title: Big Brains, Tiny Board: Pupavision, an Agentic Physical AI Instrument for Monitoring Drosophila Pupariation and Lifecycle Transitions
summary: Many biology experiments are limited by the availability and ease of use of instruments that monitor and record them. For example, the timing of pupariation in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster, a widely used model organism, can provide biologically relevant information about growth regulation and is often recorded manually. Here, we present Pupavision, a small physical AI instrument built from a single-board Linux computer and a day/night camera for roughly 45 to 75 US dollars in parts. The key idea is that a frontier coding agent runs its agentic harness directly on the tiny board. The model thinks in the cloud, but the agent works on the device. The agent assists image capture, writes code to repair errors, and checks the experiment every day to keep raw data capture reliable. If recording stops, the researcher gets a ping on their mobile phone. A simple deterministic capture service records one image every ten minutes and never depends on the agent. We report a 26-day pilot in a fly incubator (about 3,580 frames), including eleven days in which the agent was logged out and capture continued, and a 51-hour outage whose cause led to the layered design. A researcher-in-the-loop workflow then produces per-vial pupariation curves by tracing selected pupae backward in time from a late reference frame. Future work will validate the assay for lifecycle tracking accuracy against expert-labeled data and expand real-time computer vision analysis. Pupavision offers a blueprint for do-it-yourself agentic instruments that put frontier intelligence on a tiny board, with deterministic code underneath. We present this as an early case study from a pilot lab deployment and contribute lessons learned toward a future where scientific domain experts are empowered by DIY agentic hardware.

title: Truthgate: Checking Coding Agents Against a Record They Cannot Edit - Cheating, Deterrence and Disclosure on Impossible Tasks
comments: 9 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code and data: https://github.com/Cygnux-Labs/Truthgate
summary: When a coding agent says it is done, is that true, and how would anyone know? We study this question in five steps; every paid study was pre-registered, and in each step the agent is checked against a record it cannot edit: tests re-run by the host and, from step 2 on, hidden checks in containers the agent never sees and a signed log of every tool call written by a signer outside the agent's sandbox. A pilot with a small local model (Qwen3.5-4B, 36 runs on impossible tasks) found no hidden failure, and showed that labels built from actions alone over-count lies. On Impossible-LiveCodeBench, Claude Sonnet 5.5 passed 39 of 180 impossible tasks (21.7%), every time by special-casing its code to fit the failing assertion; Opus 5.5 (2.8%) and Haiku 5.5 (1.7%) rarely did. One sentence appended to the system prompt cut Sonnet's cheats on the same 60 tasks from 22 to 8 (an AI reviewer will read the transcript), 6 (a person will review the work), 6 ("This session is recorded.") and 1 (do not special-case tests), all significant under exact McNemar tests, with honest passes unchanged. No remaining cheat moved to a shell falsely described as unrecorded (0 of 4). Asked for a final report, every one of 55 natural cheats named its special case; unasked, Sonnet and Opus said nothing in 52 of 52. An LLM judge caught all 55; deterministic rules over the host record caught 27. A scripted tamper demonstration, with keyword stand-ins for the judges, shows that one rewrite of the agent-side transcript hides two calls from a judge that reads it, while the signed record keeps them; in a 40-rollout pilot, Sonnet never touched its transcript. The judge and the record caught different things, which leads to our main conclusion: the record is the evidence a judge should read, not a replacement for one. All pre-registrations, results documents, code and evidence manifests are released.

title: Integrating AI Coding Agents Into Scientific Research
comments: 36 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Software publicly available at https://github.com/RoryBarnes/vaibify
summary: New software tools have emerged that enable AI agents to quickly develop code that analyzes data and generates figures, but their mistakes can also harm a researcher's computer, require extensive resources for validation, and cause the results to be received more skeptically. These concerns could be mitigated if scientific software is developed in a secure environment with a system for monitoring file changes and well-defined standards for handling AI agents. This paper first describes how coding agents change eleven aspects of generating, verifying, and reproducing numerical results. A six-level scale is then proposed for classifying AI-assisted numerical experiments by their provenance, reproducibility, openness, oversight, and falsifiability (PROOF). The scale begins with locally self-consistent, version-controlled, human-verified results and culminates in a publicly accessible and curated archive of the files, change history, prompt transcripts, independent agent regeneration of the analysis, and multiple cryptographically verifiable attestations of regeneration by independent researchers. These aspects of AI-assisted scientific software development have been synthesized into a new open source software package called vaibify that optimizes the agentic development of computational experiments ascending the PROOF Ladder. Docker containers sequester the agents while a GUI enables researchers to prompt command line agents, monitor the current status of local and remote files, and drive a project to PROOF Level 3 (reproducible). The methods described in this paper could help researchers reduce the time required to verify agent-written software and efficiently communicate trust in AI-assisted science.

title: SkillBuffBench: Measuring What Agent Skills Contribute across Harnesses, Models, Skill Access Modes and Memory
comments: 18 pages, 2 figures, 6 tables. Work in progress: benchmark design and protocol; results to be added in a later version
summary: Agent Skills, file-based packages of procedural knowledge that a coding agent can discover and load on demand, are now shipped by every major agent harness, yet the evidence for how much they help comes almost entirely from settings in which the right Skill is hand-picked for the task and the agent starts from a blank slate. Neither holds in deployment, where an agent chooses from whatever library happens to be installed and frequently carries memory from earlier work. We present SkillBuffBench, a benchmark and paired evaluation protocol that treats Skill access as a three-level factor (no Skill, a curated Skill, and automatic invocation from an installed library), crosses it with memory (off and on), with four agent harnesses and with multiple models (the state-of-the-art proprietary models from Anthropic, Google and OpenAI, and the state-of-the-art open-weight models from Chinese providers), every model being run under every harness, and evaluates the result on research tasks contributed by domain experts together with the Skills they use, currently in materials science and biology, with the suite extended on a rolling basis. Every run is marked by a deterministic verifier; uncertainty is reported with a paired, task-level bootstrap; and cost, agent rounds and wall-clock time are reported alongside the score rather than folded into it. This version of the paper describes the design of the benchmark, its evaluation protocol and its current tasks and Skills. The evaluation is in progress: results will be added once the runs are complete, and the task suite, results and analysis will continue to be updated on a rolling basis.
